title: Probably PFC Jones, at the rotor head
description: A crewman in white T-shirt and cap — Larry believes this is PFC Jones — stands atop a Huey's fuselage at the main rotor head, cigarette in mouth, silhouetted against a bright cumulus sky; the tail of an adjacent aircraft shows at the far left edge. "Jones is  looking at a bullet hole in the rotor which causes vibration. the helicopter was vibrating really bad." The flight line, Larry says, was "probably 3 blocks away," and a de Havilland Beaver was kept there.
researchNotes: Identification relayed by Larry's son from Larry's dictation (2026-08-15 session; archived as data/recollections/giscus-vn-0012-c18035104.json and -c18035111.json), hedged as belief. Jones recurs: white-T-shirt crewman at the Huey in VN-0020, and possibly the owner of Sarge the monkey ('Jones, the helicopter pilot', VN-0017 comment). The marking on the adjacent tail at frame left is a magnification target for the unit question (ledger #2); what it shows, and every candidate reading, is kept in research/magnification/README.md and is deliberately not described in this record (2026-09-14: the description's shape reading was removed). 2026-09-03 (giscus-vn-0012-c18259673.json): Jones is looking at a bullet hole in the rotor that made the helicopter vibrate. At VN-0071 on 2026-09-05 he said 'PFC Jones and I got shot down and had to go back to the base and land one time. That is what PFC Jones was looking at in the picture' (giscus-vn-0071-c18307913.json). Jones is not in VN-0071, and this frame is the one where he says Jones is looking at damage, so 'the picture' most likely means this one; that is an inference from his two comments, not his statement, and the recollection is left linked where he posted it (ledger #34). 2026-09-12 (giscus-vn-0012-c18415667.json and -c18415677.json): 'Location: Ton Son Nhut', the flight line 'probably 3 blocks away', and a Beaver there 'made by Canadian company Dehavolond'. The aircraft brought back a story that is not a caption for this frame: he flew to Hong Kong in another de Havilland, which he could not name at first and then called the Caribou ('Not sure on spelling') — two engines on the wings, short take-off and landing, popular for short strips, 'I think they held 18 guys.' His description fits the twin-engine de Havilland Canada DHC-4 Caribou, a short take-off transport the U.S. Army flew in Vietnam in this period; that a Caribou carried him to Hong Kong is his account and is not checked, and the trip is new to the archive (ledger #38). What the trip was for is his to say; the research context is kept out of this record (research/photos/held-from-records-2026-09-14.md). The Beaver is also drawn and labelled on his 2026-09-12 sheet of the airport (VD-0004).
